beats.narration_text: Selam — Vedanshu here. Three videos, three chapters, three fixes for a RAG system. The pipeline that localises a fault. The prompt that labels what it sends. The re-ranker that re-scores a shortlist. All three work. All three stop somewhere — and the stopping point is the useful part.

beats.act: act 1 — chapter seven: the pipeline names the stage
beats.narration_text: Chapter seven built the five-stage pipeline, then broke one stage at a time. Three faults, three distinct signatures. Retrieve returns a fluent answer about the wrong policy. Augment drops the citation. Generate invents a number that is nowhere in the context. The symptom names the stage. What it does not do is fix it.

beats.act: act 2 — chapter eight: the prompt improves the odds
beats.narration_text: Chapter eight assembled the prompt deliberately. Labelled sections, each chunk tagged with its source, and one instruction to answer only from the context. That improves the odds. It does not compel. Here is the failure that survives review — a first sentence correctly grounded, and a second that quietly is not. The accurate opening is the camouflage.

props.headline: Grounded, Then Drifting.
props.instruction: Answer only using the provided context. If the context does not contain the answer, say so.

sentences.text: Two weeks of written notice is required for resignation.
Most employers also expect a handover document and an exit interview within that period.

props.warning: An accurate first sentence lends the whole answer an appearance of reliability it has not earned.
props.caption: Recap of Chapter 8. A grounding instruction is a documented technique, not a hard guarantee — it reduces the risk rather than eliminating it.

beats.act: act 3 — chapter nine: the re-ranker reorders
beats.narration_text: Chapter nine added the expensive second pass, and across six questions it promoted nothing and demoted nothing. It did reorder. But the document that answers this question was never in the top five, so the re-ranker never saw it. A re-ranker reorders what it was handed. It cannot retrieve. Stage one sets the ceiling.

beats.act: the kicker — what was measured, and what stood in
beats.narration_text: And one thing worth saying out loud across all three. Every rank, every timing, every fault signature in those videos is captured output from code that ran. But two of the three central mechanisms were stand-ins. A deterministic reader instead of a language model. Late interaction instead of a cross-encoder. Both were declared on screen, because a clean result from a stand-in is the easiest thing in the world to over-read.

beats.narration_text: So: three fixes, three ceilings. The pipeline tells you which stage broke, and stops. The prompt makes the model likelier to use what you gave it, and stops. The re-ranker orders what it was handed, and stops. None of them makes an answer true. What they buy is a system where being wrong is traceable — and that is worth more than it sounds, because the alternative is one wrong answer with no seam to open.

artifactLines: Ch. 7 — the pipeline names which stage broke. It does not repair it.
Ch. 8 — assembly improves the odds. It does not compel the model.
Ch. 9 — a re-ranker reorders. It cannot retrieve what stage 1 missed.
Each technique is bounded by something upstream of it.
None of them makes an answer true.
They make being wrong traceable — which is the whole point.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: for my RAG system, write down what each layer can and cannot fix. Then take the last ten wrong answers and say which layer should have caught each one. Run that before you add anything. Most teams buy a re-ranker when their problem is recall, or tune a prompt when their problem is retrieval. The exercise costs an afternoon, and it tells you which of these three videos you actually needed.
